questions.stem: Write the number $3\,482\,905$ in words.

questions.hint: Read the number in periods of three digits: Millions, Thousands, and Units. $3$ is in the millions period, $482$ is in the thousands, and $905$ is in the units.
questions.solution:
The number $3\,482\,905$ is grouped as:
- $3$: Three million
- $482$: four hundred and eighty-two thousand
- $905$: nine hundred and five.

Combined: 'Three million, four hundred and eighty-two thousand, nine hundred and five'.

steps.explain: Group the digits by standard three-digit periods (Millions, Thousands, Units).

steps.explain: Combine all parts with appropriate commas.
steps.work: \text{Three million, four hundred and eighty-two thousand, nine hundred and five}

- $8$ is in Thousands ($8 \times 10^3$)
- $3$ is in Hundreds ($3 \times 10^2$)

Combining these gives $405\,212$.

questions.stem: Write the number. 85 tens, 2 ones
questions.hint: Change each part into a value first (for example 85 tens = 85 × 10 = 850), then add the values.

steps.explain: Read each part of the question. 'a tens' means the number of tens; one ten is 10, one hundred is 100, one thousand is 1000.
Work out the value of 85 tens: multiply the number by the value of one ten.
Work out the value of 2 ones: multiply the number by the value of one one.
Add the values of all the parts to get the number.

questions.stem: Write the number. 300 ones
questions.hint: Change each part into a value first (for example 85 tens = 85 × 10 = 850), then add the values.

steps.explain: Read each part of the question. 'a tens' means the number of tens; one ten is 10, one hundred is 100, one thousand is 1000.
Work out the value of 300 ones: multiply the number by the value of one one.
Add the values of all the parts to get the number.

questions.stem: Write the number. 23 hundreds, 5 tens and 3 ones
questions.hint: Change each part into a value first (for example 85 tens = 85 × 10 = 850), then add the values.

steps.explain: Read each part of the question. 'a tens' means the number of tens; one ten is 10, one hundred is 100, one thousand is 1000.
Work out the value of 23 hundreds: multiply the number by the value of one hundred.
Work out the value of 5 tens: multiply the number by the value of one ten.
Work out the value of 3 ones: multiply the number by the value of one one.
Add the values of all the parts to get the number.

questions.stem: Write the number. 4 thousands, 5 hundreds and 18 ones
questions.hint: Change each part into a value first (for example 85 tens = 85 × 10 = 850), then add the values.

steps.explain: Read each part of the question. 'a tens' means the number of tens; one ten is 10, one hundred is 100, one thousand is 1000.
Work out the value of 4 thousands: multiply the number by the value of one thousand.
Work out the value of 5 hundreds: multiply the number by the value of one hundred.
Work out the value of 18 ones: multiply the number by the value of one one.
Add the values of all the parts to get the number.

questions.stem: Write the number. 128 thousands, 43 tens and 9 ones
questions.hint: Change each part into a value first (for example 85 tens = 85 × 10 = 850), then add the values.

steps.explain: Read each part of the question. 'a tens' means the number of tens; one ten is 10, one hundred is 100, one thousand is 1000.
Work out the value of 128 thousands: multiply the number by the value of one thousand.
Work out the value of 43 tens: multiply the number by the value of one ten.
Work out the value of 9 ones: multiply the number by the value of one one.
Add the values of all the parts to get the number.

questions.stem: Write the number. 17 ones, 1 ten thousand and 23 hundreds
questions.hint: Change each part into a value first (for example 85 tens = 85 × 10 = 850), then add the values.

steps.explain: Read each part of the question. 'a tens' means the number of tens; one ten is 10, one hundred is 100, one thousand is 1000.
Work out the value of 17 ones: multiply the number by the value of one one.
Work out the value of 1 ten thousand: multiply the number by the value of one ten thousand.
Work out the value of 23 hundreds: multiply the number by the value of one hundred.
Add the values of all the parts to get the number.

questions.stem: Round off the number $83\,642$ to the nearest $10\,000$.
questions.hint: Look at the digit in the thousands place (which is $3$). If it is less than $5$, round down.
questions.solution:
1. The digit in the ten-thousands place is $8$.
2. The digit to its right (thousands place) is $3$.
3. Since $3 < 5$, we round down. The $8$ remains, and all digits to the right become zero.

Result: $80\,000$.

steps.explain: Identify the digit in the rounding place (ten-thousands) and the digit immediately to its right (thousands).
Compare the check digit (thousands place) to 5. Since \(3 < 5\), round down (keep the 8 and replace subsequent numbers with zeros).

questions.stem: Round off the number $4\,517\,380$ to the nearest $10\,000$.
questions.hint: Identify the ten-thousands place (which has a $1$). Look at the digit to its right ($7$) to decide whether to round up or down.
questions.solution:
1. The ten-thousands place is $1$.
2. The digit to its right is $7$.

questions.stem: Round off the number $899\,950$ to the nearest hundred ($100$).
questions.hint: Find the hundreds digit ($9$). Look at the tens digit ($5$). Notice how rounding up triggers a chain of carrying over.
questions.solution:
1. Hundreds digit is $9$. Deciding digit (tens) is $5$, so round up.
2. Add $1$ to the hundreds place: $9 + 1 = 10$ (write $0$, carry over $1$ to the thousands place).
3. Thousands place: $9 + 1 = 10$ (write $0$, carry over $1$ to ten-thousands).
4. Ten-thousands place: $9 + 1 = 10$ (write $0$, carry over $1$ to hundred-thousands).
5. Hundred-thousands place: $8 + 1 = 9$.

Result: $900\,000$.

questions.stem: Convert the Roman numeral $CLXXIV$ to a Hindu-Arabic numeral (our standard number system).
questions.hint: Break the Roman numeral down from left to right: $C = 100$, $L = 50$, $X = 10$, and look out for subtractive pairs like $IV$.
questions.solution:
To convert $CLXXIV$:
1. $C = 100$
2. $L = 50$
3. $XX = 10 + 10 = 20$
4. $IV = 5 - 1 = 4$

Adding these together: $100 + 50 + 20 + 4 = 174$.

steps.explain: Identify the value of each individual Roman numeral symbol in the expression.
Group the symbols and check for subtractive patterns. Since \(I\) (1) is placed before \(V\) (5), it represents subtraction: \(5 - 1 = 4\).
steps.work: \begin{aligned} CLXXIV &= C + L + X + X + (V - I) \\ &= 100 + 50 + 10 + 10 + (5 - 1) \end{aligned}

steps.explain: Sum the values to find the final Hindu-Arabic numeral.

questions.stem: Convert the Roman numeral $CMXCVIII$ to a Hindu-Arabic numeral.
questions.hint: Look for subtractive pairs: $CM$ (100 before 1000) and $XC$ (10 before 100).
questions.solution:
To convert $CMXCVIII$:
1. $CM = 1000 - 100 = 900$
2. $XC = 100 - 10 = 90$
3. $VIII = 5 + 3 = 8$

Summing the values: $900 + 90 + 8 = 998$.

3. $X = 10$
4. $IX = 10 - 1 = 9$

Summing the values: $200 + 50 + 10 + 9 = 269$.

questions.stem: Express the number $840$ in Roman numerals.
questions.hint: Write the number by breaking it down into hundreds and tens: $800 + 40$. Remember $800 = 500 + 300$ and $40$ is written by subtracting $10$ from $50$.
questions.solution:
To express $840$ in Roman numerals:
1. Break it down: $800 + 40$
2. $800 = DCCC$ (500 + 100 + 100 + 100)
3. $40 = XL$ (10 subtracted from 50)

Combine the parts: $DCCCXL$.

questions.stem: Express the number $946$ in Roman numerals.
questions.hint: Break the number into $900 + 40 + 6$. Note that $900$ is written as $100$ subtracted from $1000$, and $40$ is $10$ subtracted from $50$.
questions.solution:
To express $946$ in Roman numerals:
1. Break it down: $900 + 40 + 6$
2. $900 = CM$ (1000 - 100)
3. $40 = XL$ (50 - 10)
4. $6 = VI$ (5 + 1)

Combine the parts: $CMXLVI$.

questions.stem: Write the Roman numeral in Hindu-Arabic numerals:\n\\(\text{CCLXII}\\)
questions.hint: Break down the Roman numeral into its individual values: \\(\text{C}\\), \\(\text{L}\\), \\(\text{X}\\), and \\(\text{I}\\).
questions.solution:
Convert each part of the Roman numeral \\(\text{CCLXII}\\):
- \\(\text{CC} = 100 + 100 = 200\\)
- \\(\text{L} = 50\\)
- \\(\text{X} = 10\\)
- \\(\text{II} = 1 + 1 = 2\\)

Add them together: \\(200 + 50 + 10 + 2 = 262\\).

steps.explain: Identify the values of individual Roman symbols in the string.

questions.stem: Write the Roman numeral in Hindu-Arabic numerals:\n\\(\text{CDXLIV}\\)
questions.hint: Look for subtractive pairs like \\(\text{CD}\\) (100 before 500) and \\(\text{XL}\\) (10 before 50).
questions.solution:
Convert each part of the Roman numeral \\(\text{CDXLIV}\\):
- \\(\text{CD} = 500 - 100 = 400\\)
- \\(\text{XL} = 50 - 10 = 40\\)
- \\(\text{IV} = 5 - 1 = 4\\)

Add them together: \\(400 + 40 + 4 = 444\\).

steps.explain: Identify subtractive pairs where a smaller value symbol is placed before a larger value symbol.
Sum the values of each processed group.
Calculate the final Hindu-Arabic numeral value.

questions.stem: Write the Roman numeral in Hindu-Arabic numerals:\n\\(\text{CMXCIX}\\)
questions.hint: Look for subtractive pairs like \\(\text{CM}\\), \\(\text{XC}\\), and \\(\text{IX}\\).
questions.solution:
Convert each part of the Roman numeral \\(\text{CMXCIX}\\):
- \\(\text{CM} = 1000 - 100 = 900\\)
- \\(\text{XC} = 100 - 10 = 90\\)
- \\(\text{IX} = 10 - 1 = 9\\)

Add them together: \\(900 + 90 + 9 = 999\\).

steps.explain: Identify the values of subtractive groups in \\(\text{CMXCIX}\\).
Express the total value as the sum of these grouped components.
Calculate the final result.

questions.solution:

- \\(700 = 500 + 100 + 100 = \text{DCC}\\)
- \\(30 = 10 + 10 + 10 = \text{XXX}\\)

Combine them: \\(\text{DCCXXX}\\).

questions.stem: Express the following number in Roman numerals:\n\\(934\\)
questions.hint: Break down 934 into place values: \\(900 + 30 + 4\\). Note that 900 is written by subtracting 100 from 1000.
questions.solution:
Convert each part of \\(934\\) to Roman numerals:
- \\(900 = 1000 - 100 = \text{CM}\\)
- \\(30 = 10 + 10 + 10 = \text{XXX}\\)
- \\(4 = 5 - 1 = \text{IV}\\)

Combine them: \\(\text{CMXXXIV}\\).

steps.explain: Separate the decimal number into place values.

Assemble the final Roman numeral string.

questions.stem: Express the following number in Roman numerals:\n\\(1989\\)
questions.hint: Break down 1989 into place values: \\(1000 + 900 + 80 + 9\\).
questions.solution:
Convert each part of \\(1989\\) to Roman numerals:
- \\(1000 = \text{M}\\)
- \\(900 = 1000 - 100 = \text{CM}\\)
- \\(80 = 50 + 10 + 10 + 10 = \text{LXXX}\\)
- \\(9 = 10 - 1 = \text{IX}\\)

Combine them: \\(\text{MCMLXXXIX}\\).

Join the parts in order from largest value to smallest.

steps.explain: Check with a shortcut: the 10th number needs 9 jumps of 6, so it should be the start + 9×6.
Why the other answers are wrong: one list leaves out the starting number, another uses the wrong jump size, and another counts in the opposite direction.

keyPoints.note: Add (forwards) or subtract (backwards) the same jump each time.
Check the last term: start ± (number of jumps × jump size).

meta.source: ICE-EM Mathematics Year 6 (3rd ed.) Chapter 1: Positive and negative whole numbers
meta.note: Buzz game. The textbook says 'buzz' for numbers in the counting pattern; the question here asks for the numbers of the pattern.

questions.stem: Buzz forwards: Count by nines from 0. Which list shows the first 10 numbers of this counting pattern?
questions.hint: Start at 0 and add 9 each time. The starting number is the FIRST number in the list.

steps.explain: Read the question: counting forwards (the numbers get bigger) by 9s, starting at 0. So we start at 0 and add 9 each time.

steps.explain: Check with a shortcut: the 10th number needs 9 jumps of 9, so it should be the start + 9×9.
Why the other answers are wrong: one list leaves out the starting number, another uses the wrong jump size, and another counts in the opposite direction.

keyPoints.note: Add (forwards) or subtract (backwards) the same jump each time.
Check the last term: start ± (number of jumps × jump size).

meta.source: ICE-EM Mathematics Year 6 (3rd ed.) Chapter 1: Positive and negative whole numbers
meta.note: Buzz game. The textbook says 'buzz' for numbers in the counting pattern; the question here asks for the numbers of the pattern.

questions.stem: Buzz forwards: Count by sixes from 15. Which list shows the first 10 numbers of this counting pattern?
questions.hint: Start at 15 and add 6 each time. The starting number is the FIRST number in the list.

steps.explain: Read the question: counting forwards (the numbers get bigger) by 6s, starting at 15. So we start at 15 and add 6 each time.

steps.explain: Check with a shortcut: the 10th number needs 9 jumps of 6, so it should be the start + 9×6.
Why the other answers are wrong: one list leaves out the starting number, another uses the wrong jump size, and another counts in the opposite direction.

keyPoints.note: Add (forwards) or subtract (backwards) the same jump each time.
Check the last term: start ± (number of jumps × jump size).

meta.source: ICE-EM Mathematics Year 6 (3rd ed.) Chapter 1: Positive and negative whole numbers
meta.note: Buzz game. The textbook says 'buzz' for numbers in the counting pattern; the question here asks for the numbers of the pattern.

questions.stem: Buzz forwards: Count by nines from 121. Which list shows the first 10 numbers of this counting pattern?
questions.hint: Start at 121 and add 9 each time. The starting number is the FIRST number in the list.

steps.explain: Read the question: counting forwards (the numbers get bigger) by 9s, starting at 121. So we start at 121 and add 9 each time.

steps.explain: Check with a shortcut: the 10th number needs 9 jumps of 9, so it should be the start + 9×9.
Why the other answers are wrong: one list leaves out the starting number, another uses the wrong jump size, and another counts in the opposite direction.

keyPoints.note: Add (forwards) or subtract (backwards) the same jump each time.
Check the last term: start ± (number of jumps × jump size).

meta.source: ICE-EM Mathematics Year 6 (3rd ed.) Chapter 1: Positive and negative whole numbers
meta.note: Buzz game. The textbook says 'buzz' for numbers in the counting pattern; the question here asks for the numbers of the pattern.

questions.stem: Buzz backwards: Count backwards by fours from 100. Which list shows the first 10 numbers of this counting pattern?
questions.hint: Start at 100 and subtract 4 each time. The starting number is the FIRST number in the list.

steps.explain: Check with a shortcut: the 10th number needs 9 jumps of 4, so it should be the start - 9×4.
Why the other answers are wrong: one list leaves out the starting number, another uses the wrong jump size, and another counts in the opposite direction.

keyPoints.note: Add (forwards) or subtract (backwards) the same jump each time.
Check the last term: start ± (number of jumps × jump size).

meta.source: ICE-EM Mathematics Year 6 (3rd ed.) Chapter 1: Positive and negative whole numbers
meta.note: Buzz game. The textbook says 'buzz' for numbers in the counting pattern; the question here asks for the numbers of the pattern.

questions.stem: Buzz backwards: Count backwards by elevens from 100. Which list shows the first 10 numbers of this counting pattern?
questions.hint: Start at 100 and subtract 11 each time. The starting number is the FIRST number in the list.

steps.explain: Read the question: counting backwards (the numbers get smaller) by 11s, starting at 100. So we start at 100 and subtract 11 each time.

steps.explain: Check with a shortcut: the 10th number needs 9 jumps of 11, so it should be the start - 9×11.
Why the other answers are wrong: one list leaves out the starting number, another uses the wrong jump size, and another counts in the opposite direction.

keyPoints.note: Add (forwards) or subtract (backwards) the same jump each time.
Check the last term: start ± (number of jumps × jump size).

meta.source: ICE-EM Mathematics Year 6 (3rd ed.) Chapter 1: Positive and negative whole numbers
meta.note: Buzz game. The textbook says 'buzz' for numbers in the counting pattern; the question here asks for the numbers of the pattern.

questions.stem: Buzz backwards: Count backwards by sevens from 1000. Which list shows the first 10 numbers of this counting pattern?
questions.hint: Start at 1000 and subtract 7 each time. The starting number is the FIRST number in the list.

steps.explain: Read the question: counting backwards (the numbers get smaller) by 7s, starting at 1000. So we start at 1000 and subtract 7 each time.

steps.explain: Check with a shortcut: the 10th number needs 9 jumps of 7, so it should be the start - 9×7.
Why the other answers are wrong: one list leaves out the starting number, another uses the wrong jump size, and another counts in the opposite direction.

keyPoints.note: Add (forwards) or subtract (backwards) the same jump each time.
Check the last term: start ± (number of jumps × jump size).

meta.source: ICE-EM Mathematics Year 6 (3rd ed.) Chapter 1: Positive and negative whole numbers
meta.note: Buzz game. The textbook says 'buzz' for numbers in the counting pattern; the question here asks for the numbers of the pattern.

questions.stem: Buzz backwards: Count backwards by twelves from 170. Which list shows the first 10 numbers of this counting pattern?
questions.hint: Start at 170 and subtract 12 each time. The starting number is the FIRST number in the list.

steps.explain: Read the question: counting backwards (the numbers get smaller) by 12s, starting at 170. So we start at 170 and subtract 12 each time.

steps.explain: Check with a shortcut: the 10th number needs 9 jumps of 12, so it should be the start - 9×12.
Why the other answers are wrong: one list leaves out the starting number, another uses the wrong jump size, and another counts in the opposite direction.

keyPoints.note: Add (forwards) or subtract (backwards) the same jump each time.
Check the last term: start ± (number of jumps × jump size).

meta.source: ICE-EM Mathematics Year 6 (3rd ed.) Chapter 1: Positive and negative whole numbers
meta.note: Buzz game. The textbook says 'buzz' for numbers in the counting pattern; the question here asks for the numbers of the pattern.

questions.stem: Beachball: Start at 0 and count forwards by threes. Which list shows the first 10 numbers of this counting pattern?
questions.hint: Start at 0 and add 3 each time. The starting number is the FIRST number in the list.

steps.explain: Read the question: counting forwards (the numbers get bigger) by 3s, starting at 0. So we start at 0 and add 3 each time.

Why the other answers are wrong: one list leaves out the starting number, another uses the wrong jump size, and another counts in the opposite direction.

keyPoints.note: Add (forwards) or subtract (backwards) the same jump each time.
The starting number is the first number in the list.

meta.source: ICE-EM Mathematics Year 6 (3rd ed.) Chapter 1: Positive and negative whole numbers

questions.stem: Beachball: Start at 3 and count forwards by sevens. Which list shows the first 10 numbers of this counting pattern?
questions.hint: Start at 3 and add 7 each time. The starting number is the FIRST number in the list.

steps.explain: Check with a shortcut: the 10th number needs 9 jumps of 7, so it should be the start + 9×7.
Why the other answers are wrong: one list leaves out the starting number, another uses the wrong jump size, and another counts in the opposite direction.

keyPoints.note: Add (forwards) or subtract (backwards) the same jump each time.
The starting number is the first number in the list.

meta.source: ICE-EM Mathematics Year 6 (3rd ed.) Chapter 1: Positive and negative whole numbers

questions.stem: Beachball: Start at 1000 and count backwards by fours. Which list shows the first 10 numbers of this counting pattern?
questions.hint: Start at 1000 and subtract 4 each time. The starting number is the FIRST number in the list.

steps.explain: Read the question: counting backwards (the numbers get smaller) by 4s, starting at 1000. So we start at 1000 and subtract 4 each time.

Why the other answers are wrong: one list leaves out the starting number, another uses the wrong jump size, and another counts in the opposite direction.

keyPoints.note: Add (forwards) or subtract (backwards) the same jump each time.
The starting number is the first number in the list.

meta.source: ICE-EM Mathematics Year 6 (3rd ed.) Chapter 1: Positive and negative whole numbers

questions.stem: Beachball: Start at 889 and count backwards by eights. Which list shows the first 10 numbers of this counting pattern?
questions.hint: Start at 889 and subtract 8 each time. The starting number is the FIRST number in the list.

steps.explain: Read the question: counting backwards (the numbers get smaller) by 8s, starting at 889. So we start at 889 and subtract 8 each time.

Why the other answers are wrong: one list leaves out the starting number, another uses the wrong jump size, and another counts in the opposite direction.

keyPoints.note: Add (forwards) or subtract (backwards) the same jump each time.
The starting number is the first number in the list.

meta.source: ICE-EM Mathematics Year 6 (3rd ed.) Chapter 1: Positive and negative whole numbers

questions.stem: Beachball: Start at 56 and count forwards by thirteens. Which list shows the first 10 numbers of this counting pattern?
questions.hint: Start at 56 and add 13 each time. The starting number is the FIRST number in the list.

steps.explain: Read the question: counting forwards (the numbers get bigger) by 13s, starting at 56. So we start at 56 and add 13 each time.

steps.explain: Check with a shortcut: the 10th number needs 9 jumps of 4, so it should be the start - 9×4.
Why the other answers are wrong: one list leaves out the starting number, another uses the wrong jump size, and another counts in the opposite direction.

keyPoints.note: Add (forwards) or subtract (backwards) the same jump each time.
The starting number is the first number in the list.
Check the last term: start ± (number of jumps × jump size).

meta.source: ICE-EM Mathematics Year 6 (3rd ed.) Chapter 1: Positive and negative whole numbers

questions.stem: For each counting sequence, write as many numbers as you can in 2 minutes. Count forwards by sevens, starting at 99. Which list shows the first 10 numbers?
questions.hint: Start at 99 and add 7 each time. The starting number is the FIRST number in the list.

steps.explain: Check with a shortcut: the 10th number needs 9 jumps of 7, so it should be the start + 9×7.
Why the other answers are wrong: one list leaves out the starting number, another uses the wrong jump size, and another counts in the opposite direction.

keyPoints.note: Add (forwards) or subtract (backwards) the same jump each time.
The starting number is the first number in the list.
Check the last term: start ± (number of jumps × jump size).

questions.stem: For each counting sequence, write as many numbers as you can in 2 minutes. Count forwards by nines, starting at 346. Which list shows the first 10 numbers?
questions.hint: Start at 346 and add 9 each time. The starting number is the FIRST number in the list.

steps.explain: Check with a shortcut: the 10th number needs 9 jumps of 9, so it should be the start + 9×9.
Why the other answers are wrong: one list leaves out the starting number, another uses the wrong jump size, and another counts in the opposite direction.

keyPoints.note: Add (forwards) or subtract (backwards) the same jump each time.
The starting number is the first number in the list.
Check the last term: start ± (number of jumps × jump size).

questions.stem: For each counting sequence, write as many numbers as you can in 2 minutes. Count backwards by eights, starting at 1777. Which list shows the first 10 numbers?
questions.hint: Start at 1777 and subtract 8 each time. The starting number is the FIRST number in the list.

steps.explain: Check with a shortcut: the 10th number needs 9 jumps of 8, so it should be the start - 9×8.
Why the other answers are wrong: one list leaves out the starting number, another uses the wrong jump size, and another counts in the opposite direction.

keyPoints.note: Add (forwards) or subtract (backwards) the same jump each time.
The starting number is the first number in the list.
Check the last term: start ± (number of jumps × jump size).

meta.note: The textbook asks for as many numbers as possible in 2 minutes; the question asks for the first 10 numbers.

questions.stem: List the first 20 numbers in the counting sequence for each of the numbers in the pair, starting with the number itself. Then highlight the numbers that are the same in both lists. Which numbers are the same in both lists? \(2\ \text{and}\ 3\)
questions.hint: Write the multiples of 2 and the multiples of 3. The numbers in both lists are the ones to highlight - find the first one, then keep adding it.

The other shared numbers are found by adding 6 each time: 6, 12, 18, 24, 30, 36.
Why the other answers are wrong: one lists only the first shared number, another lists the first numbers of only ONE counting sequence, and another leaves out a shared number.

keyPoints.note: Shared numbers appear in both lists.
The first shared number repeats at equal gaps.

The other shared numbers are found by adding 12 each time: 12, 24, 36, 48, 60.
Why the other answers are wrong: one lists only the first shared number, another lists the first numbers of only ONE counting sequence, and another leaves out a shared number.

keyPoints.note: Shared numbers appear in both lists.
The first shared number repeats at equal gaps.

The other shared numbers are found by adding 20 each time: 20, 40, 60, 80.

The first shared number repeats at equal gaps.

questions.stem: List the first 20 numbers in the counting sequence for each of the numbers in the pair, starting with the number itself. Then highlight the numbers that are the same in both lists. Which numbers are the same in both lists? \(3\ \text{and}\ 8\)

steps.explain: The first shared number is 24. It is in both lists because it is a multiple of 3 (24) and a multiple of 8.
The other shared numbers are found by adding 24 each time: 24, 48.
Why the other answers are wrong: one lists only the first shared number, another lists the first numbers of only ONE counting sequence, and another leaves out a shared number.

keyPoints.note: Shared numbers appear in both lists.
The first shared number repeats at equal gaps.

meta.source: ICE-EM Mathematics Year 6 (3rd ed.) Chapter 1: Positive and negative whole numbers
meta.note: Textbook Q3 (part a is the worked example).

questions.stem: List the first 20 numbers in the counting sequence for each of the numbers in the pair, starting with the number itself. Then highlight the numbers that are the same in both lists. Which numbers are the same in both lists? \(8\ \text{and}\ 9\)
questions.hint: Write the multiples of 8 and the multiples of 9. The numbers in both lists are the ones to highlight - find the first one, then keep adding it.

steps.explain: List the first 20 numbers of the counting sequence for 8: start at 8 and add 8 each time.

questions.stem: What did you notice about the numbers that were the same in both lists in the question above? Write the first 5 numbers that will be the same in the counting sequences for 4 and 9 without writing the list for each number.
questions.hint: Find the FIRST number in both sequences (multiply 4 × 9), then keep adding it.

steps.explain: Look back at the earlier pairs: the shared numbers are spaced equally. For 2 and 3 they were 6, 12, 18, 24, 30, 36 - they go up by 6, and 6 = 2 × 3 is the FIRST shared number.
For 4 and 9 the first shared number is the smallest number that is in both the 4-sequence and the 9-sequence. 4 and 9 have no common factor, so it is 4 × 9.
Check 36 is in both sequences: it is 9 fours and 4 nines.
The shared numbers go up by 36 each time (the first shared number), so add 36 four more times.

meta.source: ICE-EM Mathematics Year 6 (3rd ed.) Chapter 1: Positive and negative whole numbers
meta.note: Ladder drawn from 9 to -9 as in the textbook.

questions.stem: Make a number ladder that goes from −100 to 100. Use the ladder and some clothes pegs to show how many steps it is from: 2 to −3. How many steps is it?
questions.hint: Mark both numbers on a number line. If they are on opposite sides of 0, add the steps to 0 and the steps from 0. If they are on the same side, subtract.

steps.explain: Mark both numbers on a number line: 2 (red) and −3 (green). The 'steps' are the equal jumps from one to the other.

steps.explain: So it takes 4 steps to go from −1 to 3.

Why the other answers are wrong: subtracting the sizes when the numbers are on opposite sides of 0 (or adding them when they are on the same side) gives a different number; being one step out comes from counting the numbers instead of the jumps.

keyPoints.note: Draw both numbers on a number line.
Count jumps, not numbers.

meta.note: The ladder/pegs activity is turned into a question: how many steps.

questions.stem: Make a number ladder that goes from −100 to 100. Use the ladder and some clothes pegs to show how many steps it is from: 5 to −5. How many steps is it?
questions.hint: Mark both numbers on a number line. If they are on opposite sides of 0, add the steps to 0 and the steps from 0. If they are on the same side, subtract.

steps.explain: Mark both numbers on a number line: 5 (red) and −5 (green). The 'steps' are the equal jumps from one to the other.

steps.explain: So it takes 10 steps to go from 5 to −5.

Why the other answers are wrong: subtracting the sizes when the numbers are on opposite sides of 0 (or adding them when they are on the same side) gives a different number; being one step out comes from counting the numbers instead of the jumps.

keyPoints.note: Draw both numbers on a number line.
Count jumps, not numbers.

meta.source: ICE-EM Mathematics Year 6 (3rd ed.) Chapter 1: Positive and negative whole numbers
meta.note: The ladder/pegs activity is turned into a question: how many steps.

questions.stem: Make a number ladder that goes from −100 to 100. Use the ladder and some clothes pegs to show how many steps it is from: −6 to −10. How many steps is it?
questions.hint: Mark both numbers on a number line. If they are on opposite sides of 0, add the steps to 0 and the steps from 0. If they are on the same side, subtract.

steps.explain: Mark both numbers on a number line: −6 (red) and −10 (green). The 'steps' are the equal jumps from one to the other.

questions.stem: This sequence is going down by twos: 4, 2, 0, −2, −4, −6. Write the next 5 integers in the sequence.
questions.hint: Going down by twos means subtract 2 each time. Carry on from -6.

steps.explain: Find the pattern: each number is 2 LESS than the one before it.

steps.explain: Check: compare each pair of neighbours in your final list. Each number must be larger than the one after it.

Why the other answers are wrong: one list is in the opposite order; one sorts by size ignoring the minus signs (so -23 looks bigger than -2); one swaps two neighbours; one puts the negatives in the wrong order.

keyPoints.note: Negative numbers are smaller than zero and than positive numbers.
Furthest right is largest.
Negatives are left of 0.

keyPoints.note: Equal steps between marks.
Count the step size between marks.
Negative integers are left of 0.

questions.stem: List the integers that are: between 0 and −5
questions.hint: Draw the two end numbers as empty circles. The answers are the whole numbers (integers) strictly between them, listed from left to right.

steps.explain: Mark the two end numbers −5 and 0 on a number line. They are NOT in the list, because the question says smaller than / larger than (or between): so we draw them as empty circles.

Why the other answers are wrong: one includes the end numbers, one leaves out the first, one leaves out the last, and one shifts the whole list by one place.

keyPoints.note: List from smallest to largest.
Integers include negative numbers, zero and positive numbers.
End numbers are not included.

meta.source: ICE-EM Mathematics Year 6 (3rd ed.) Chapter 1: Positive and negative whole numbers

questions.stem: List the integers that are: smaller than 3 but larger than −10
questions.hint: Draw the two end numbers as empty circles. The answers are the whole numbers (integers) strictly between them, listed from left to right.

steps.explain: Mark the two end numbers −10 and 3 on a number line. They are NOT in the list, because the question says smaller than / larger than (or between): so we draw them as empty circles.

steps.explain: The value of a digit is the digit multiplied by the value of its place.
Write the answer with its name: 4 tens of millions is 40 000 000.
Check with expanded form: split the whole number into the value of each digit. The highlighted part is the one we found.

Why the other answers are wrong: 4 on its own is the DIGIT, not its value; a value that is ten times too big or ten times too small means a place was counted wrongly (check the digits to the right again).

keyPoints.note: The value of a digit = the digit × the value of its place.
Count the digits to its right to find its place.

questions.stem: Write the first 10 numbers in each counting sequence. Count forwards by ones, starting at 691.
questions.hint: Start at 691 and add 1 each time. The starting number is the FIRST number in the list.

steps.explain: Read the question: counting forwards (the numbers get bigger) by 1s, starting at 691. So we start at 691 and add 1 each time.

keyPoints.note: Add (forwards) or subtract (backwards) the same jump each time.
The starting number is the first number in the list.
Check the last term: start ± (number of jumps × jump size).

keyPoints.note: Add (forwards) or subtract (backwards) the same jump each time.
The starting number is the first number in the list.
Check the last term: start ± (number of jumps × jump size).

The starting number is the first number in the list.
Check the last term: start ± (number of jumps × jump size).

keyPoints.note: Add (forwards) or subtract (backwards) the same jump each time.
The starting number is the first number in the list.
Check the last term: start ± (number of jumps × jump size).

Why the other answers are wrong: one list leaves out the starting number, another uses the wrong jump size, and another counts in the opposite direction.

keyPoints.note: Add (forwards) or subtract (backwards) the same jump each time.
The starting number is the first number in the list.
Check the last term: start ± (number of jumps × jump size).

meta.source: ICE-EM Mathematics Year 6 (3rd ed.) Chapter 1: Positive and negative whole numbers

Why the other answers are wrong: one list leaves out the starting number, another uses the wrong jump size, and another counts in the opposite direction.

keyPoints.note: Add (forwards) or subtract (backwards) the same jump each time.
The starting number is the first number in the list.
Check the last term: start ± (number of jumps × jump size).

meta.source: ICE-EM Mathematics Year 6 (3rd ed.) Chapter 1: Positive and negative whole numbers

questions.hint: Start at 87 and add 8 each time. The starting number is the FIRST number in the list.

keyPoints.note: Add (forwards) or subtract (backwards) the same jump each time.
The starting number is the first number in the list.
Check the last term: start ± (number of jumps × jump size).

keyPoints.note: Add (forwards) or subtract (backwards) the same jump each time.
The starting number is the first number in the list.
Check the last term: start ± (number of jumps × jump size).
